20 Long-Distance Relationship Activities

Most long-distance advice is about communicating better. But these relationships rarely struggle from too little talking - they struggle because talking is all there is.

Kishan Naik
August 6, 2026 6 min read

In this article

  1. Why calls alone are not enough
  2. Seven things that take five minutes
  3. Seven things for an evening
  4. Six things that build over months
  5. Managing the time difference
  6. What long distance is actually hard at
  7. Start with one small thing

The advice given to long-distance couples is almost always about communication. Talk more. Schedule calls. Be honest about your feelings. It is reasonable advice and it addresses the wrong problem, because most long-distance relationships do not fail from insufficient talking.

They struggle because talking is the only thing available. Couples who live together spend most of their time in parallel rather than in conversation - cooking while the other reads, walking somewhere, sitting in the same room doing separate things. That parallel time is where a great deal of intimacy actually lives, and distance removes it entirely.

So the useful question is not how to communicate better. It is what to do together when you cannot be together. These 20 activities are answers to that, sorted by how much time they take.

Why calls alone are not enough

A video call is high-bandwidth conversation and nothing else. It requires constant active attention, it has no natural rhythm of silence, and - the part people notice least - it produces nothing.

A call ends and leaves no evidence it happened. There is no artefact, no photograph, no object. Over months of a long-distance relationship this accumulates into a strange sensation that the relationship exists mostly as a series of conversations you cannot quite remember.

Shared activities fix both problems at once. They remove the pressure to fill silence, and many of them leave something behind. That second part matters more than it sounds - it is the difference between a relationship you can point at and one you can only describe.

A useful test for any long-distance activity: does it produce something? A film watched together produces a memory. A photo strip taken together produces an object. Both are good; the second one survives.

Seven things that take five minutes

Small, repeatable, and far more sustainable than an elaborate plan nobody keeps up.

1The daily strip

One photo strip a day, sent without comment. Not staged, not flattering - whatever you are doing at the time. Over a month it becomes a genuinely detailed picture of each other's ordinary life, which is precisely what distance takes away.

2Your window, every morning

A photograph of what is outside. Weather, light, season. It tells them where you actually are in a way describing it never manages.

3The same question, daily

Pick one question and ask it every day for a month. "Best thing that happened today." "One thing you noticed." The repetition is what makes it work - variety would make it a chore.

4A photograph of what you are eating

Unremarkable and unexpectedly effective. Meals are the most regular structure in a day and the thing you would otherwise share automatically.

5Voice notes instead of texts

A ninety-second voice note carries tone, hesitation and background noise. Text carries none of those. It is the cheapest available upgrade in intimacy per unit of effort. For one worth keeping rather than losing in a chat thread, try turning it into a digital cassette.

6The shared note

One document both of you can edit. Add to it whenever. No obligation to respond. It becomes a slow, ongoing conversation with no pressure attached.

7Goodnight at their time

If the gap is large, send a goodnight aligned to their night rather than yours. A small acknowledgement that their day has a different shape.

Seven things for an evening

8Cook the same meal

Same recipe, same time, both cameras on, minimal talking. This is the closest available substitute for parallel time - you are doing a thing, together, and conversation happens around it rather than instead of it.

9A shared photo strip

Both of you on one strip, from two cities. It takes about a minute and it produces the object that a call does not. This is what the shared booth was built for.

10Read the same thing aloud

A chapter each, alternating. Slow, old-fashioned, and one of the few activities that genuinely works better on a call than in person.

11The walk

Both go for a walk at the same time, on the phone, cameras off. No screen, no eye contact, just walking and talking. Long-distance couples consistently report this as the thing that most closely resembles being together.

12Games that are not games night

Chess, crosswords, anything asynchronous. The value is in having an ongoing thing rather than in the game itself.

13Watch something in silence

Synchronised, on a call, without commentary. The point is the shared experience, not the discussion of it. Talking through a film is a different activity.

14Plan the next visit

An evening spent on logistics sounds unromantic and is one of the most reliably good things a long-distance couple can do. It converts an abstract future into a dated one.

There are twenty-five more in 25 virtual date ideas that are actually fun.

Six things that build over months

These are the ones that matter most, because they create a record. Long-distance relationships suffer from having no visible history, and a record is how you fix that.

15The monthly strip

One shared photo strip a month, same day each month. After a year you have twelve objects that show the relationship existing across time. Nothing else on this list produces that.

16The countdown

A strip each month holding the number of weeks until you next see each other. Watching the number go down is a surprisingly effective piece of psychology.

17Letters, on paper, posted

Slow, physical, and qualitatively different from anything digital. A letter that took four days to arrive carries an implicit statement about effort that a message cannot. A digital love letter keeps the same folding-and-sealing ritual, with photos attached, if four days is more delay than you want.

18A shared album

One place both of you add to. Not a chat, not a feed - an album with a beginning. Over a year it becomes the visual history the relationship otherwise lacks.

19The same book, slowly

A chapter a week each, discussed whenever. It gives you a shared reference point that is not the relationship itself, which is more valuable than it sounds.

20One tradition with a date

Anything, as long as it is fixed. The first Sunday of the month. The 14th. What matters is that it recurs without being organised each time, which is the only way anything survives a busy month. There is more on this in how to start a photo strip tradition.

Managing the time difference

Time zones are the practical constraint that shapes everything else, and most couples handle them by trying to force an overlap that does not comfortably exist.

  • Find the real overlap and protect it. Usually one or two hours. Treat that window as the relationship's actual time together and do not fill it with admin.
  • Use asynchronous activities for the rest. Voice notes, shared documents, separate strips of the same prompt. These do not require simultaneity and therefore never get cancelled.
  • Do not always sacrifice the same person's sleep. Alternate who takes the awkward hour. Resentment about this accumulates quietly and is rarely raised directly.
  • Name the times out loud. "It is 9pm here, 4pm there" at the start of a call. It sounds trivial and it consistently reduces the number of misunderstandings about why someone is tired or distracted.

What long distance is actually hard at

It is worth being precise about which parts are difficult, because couples often blame themselves for struggling with something structural.

Ordinary time is the hard part. Big occasions are fine - birthdays and visits get planned and celebrated properly. What disappears is the unremarkable middle, and that is most of a relationship.

Silence stops being comfortable. Living together, silence is neutral. On a call it reads as something being wrong, which puts pressure on every conversation to be interesting.

You lose the ability to notice. In person you can see somebody has had a bad day before they say anything. On a scheduled call, they have had hours to arrange their face.

Activities help with all three, and specifically with the first. The daily strip, the same meal, the parallel walk - none of them are romantic gestures. They are ways of manufacturing ordinary time, which is the thing distance actually takes.

Start with one small thing

The most common mistake is starting six of these at once, keeping them up for two weeks, and then abandoning all of them. A single sustainable habit beats an elaborate system every time.

Pick one from the five-minute list and do it for a month. If it survives a month it will probably survive a year, and one thing you actually do is worth more than five you intended to.

If you want the one with the highest return, it is the monthly shared strip. Ninety seconds, once a month, and after a year you have something that shows the relationship existed in a form you can hold. The booth works from a link, in any browser, in both countries.

Frequently Asked Questions

What can long-distance couples do together?

The most sustainable options are small and repeatable: a daily photo strip sent without comment, a photograph of what is outside your window, or the same question asked every day for a month. For an evening, cooking the same meal simultaneously or going for a walk on the phone with cameras off both work well.

Why do video calls not feel like enough?

A call is high-bandwidth conversation and nothing else. Couples who live together spend most of their time in parallel rather than talking, and that parallel time is where a lot of intimacy lives. Calls also produce no artefact - they end and leave no evidence they happened.

How do you handle a big time difference in a relationship?

Find the genuine overlap, usually one or two hours, and protect it rather than filling it with admin. Use asynchronous activities for everything else so they never get cancelled. Alternate who takes the awkward hour, since always sacrificing the same person's sleep builds quiet resentment.

What is the hardest part of a long-distance relationship?

Ordinary time. Big occasions get planned and celebrated properly; what disappears is the unremarkable middle, which is most of a relationship. Silence also stops being comfortable on a call, and you lose the ability to notice someone has had a bad day before they say so.

How do you keep a long-distance ritual going?

Start one thing rather than six. The common failure is beginning several at once, sustaining them for a fortnight and abandoning all of them. Attach the ritual to a fixed date so it recurs without needing to be organised each time, and give it a month before judging whether it works.

How can long-distance couples take pictures together while apart?
